nameStory: This cheerful plant gets its name from its notably large, pink flowers that stand out among the woodsorrel family - most of which have tiny yellow blooms. The 'sorrel' part comes from the French word 'surelle' meaning sour, referring to the tangy, lemony taste of its leaves that's caused by oxalic acid.
description: Largeflower pink-sorrel is a low-growing perennial herb with distinctive three-part leaves that look like tiny shamrocks. It produces showy pink flowers that are unusually large for a woodsorrel, typically growing in small clusters. This South American native has spread around the world and occasionally pops up in New England gardens and disturbed areas, forming small patches through underground bulbs.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink flowers with five petals that are notably larger than other woodsorrels - about the size of a nickel. The petals have a silky texture and often show darker pink veins when you look closely.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Classic shamrock-shaped leaves divided into three heart-shaped leaflets that fold downward at night or when touched. The leaves taste distinctly sour and lemony when chewed, like a mild version of rhubarb.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mats or small colonies, rarely growing taller than 6 inches. The stems are soft and somewhat fleshy, often with a reddish tinge at the base.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small, pointed capsules that split open explosively when ripe, shooting tiny seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop' if you disturb them.

habitat: In New England, this species is quite rare and typically found in disturbed soils around gardens, greenhouses, or areas where soil has been imported. It prefers well-drained, slightly sandy soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade. Look for it near cultivated areas rather than in wild natural habitats.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from underground bulbs, with fresh shamrock-like leaves appearing first. Early flowers may begin blooming in late spring if conditions are warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering period with bright pink blooms most abundant in early to mid-summer. The plant remains actively growing and may continue producing flowers sporadically.
seasonality.fall: Flowering often continues into early fall, though less abundantly. Leaves may develop reddish tints as temperatures cool, and seed capsules mature and release.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground bulbs in cold areas, leaving little trace above ground. In protected microclimates, some leaves may persist through mild winters.

funFact: This plant is like nature's tiny cannon - when the seed pods ripen, they explode at the slightest touch, launching seeds up to 10 feet away! Kids love gently touching the plump, pointed pods to watch them 'pop' and scatter their contents.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with violet woodsorrel, but violet woodsorrel has true purple flowers while this species has pink blooms. The much more common yellow woodsorrels are easy to distinguish by their tiny yellow flowers instead of the large pink ones.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pink-sorrel,' this plant isn't related to true sorrels in the buckwheat family - it just shares the same sour taste. The leaves, flowers, and roots are all edible and make a tangy addition to salads, though eating large quantities isn't recommended due to the oxalic acid content.
compareHints: Among New England's woodsorrels, this is the only one with large pink flowers - all the others have either small yellow blooms or purple ones. The flowers are at least twice the size of any yellow woodsorrel, making identification straightforward when in bloom. When not flowering, the somewhat fleshy stems and tendency to grow from bulbs rather than spreading runners helps distinguish it from the more common native species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mountain woodsorrel differs from its yellow-flowered relatives in the genus by having white petals with pink veins instead of bright yellow ones.
Among New England's woodsorrels, upright yellow woodsorrel stands tall while creeping woodsorrel sprawls flat along the ground.
Slender yellow woodsorrel is smaller and more delicate than upright yellow woodsorrel, with thinner stems that tend to sprawl rather than stand erect.
Creeping woodsorrel differs from its upright cousin (Oxalis stricta) mainly in its prostrate, mat-forming growth habit versus the upright's tall, erect stems.
Violet wood-sorrel is easily distinguished from its New England relatives by its purple flowers - all other common wood-sorrels in the region have yellow flowers.
Unlike other woodsorrels in New England which have green leaves and yellow flowers, false shamrock stands out with its deep maroon foliage and white or pink blooms.
Great yellow woodsorrel differs from its more common relatives like upright yellow woodsorrel and slender yellow woodsorrel by its significantly larger leaflets and more spreading growth habit.
Pink-sorrel stands out from New England's other woodsorrels primarily by its pink flowers - most relatives have yellow blooms, while violet woodsorrel has purple flowers.
